In this eye-opening talk at the DEF CON 27 TransportHax Village, Tarah Wheeler investigates severe privacy vulnerabilities and cybersecurity oversights embedded within civil aviation pilot training programs. She begins at 04:00 by recounting her personal experience learning to fly open-cockpit vintage aircraft like the de Havilland DH.60 Tiger Moth, noting the profound contrast between archaic mechanical flying and modern electronic aviation administration.

At 08:00, Tarah reviews federal aviation regulations, outlining the legal obligations pilots face regarding flight safety and passenger oversight. She reveals a critical data privacy failure at 12:00 within the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Airmen Certification Registry, showing how public databases expose student and commercial pilots' full legal names, home street addresses, medical certificate tiers, and pilot ratings to anyone on the internet without authentication.

Tarah highlights the dangerous threat modeling implications at 16:00, illustrating how stalkers and hostile actors can correlate real-time public ADS-B flight-tracking data with FAA registry records at 20:00 to track student pilots from departure to their home doorsteps. She concludes at 24:00 by calling on the FAA and regulatory bodies to modernize aviation privacy standards, restrict open access to personal identifying information, and protect general aviation aviators from digital harassment. Zoltan Madarassy provides a comprehensive technical overview of commercial aircraft cybersecurity engineering, walking through the architecture, communication buses, and security assessment methodologies applied to modern aviation systems.

[06:44] Madarassy outlines the core security domains established under standard avionics architectures: the Aircraft Control Domain (ACD) responsible for flight-critical operations, the Airline Information Services Domain (AISD) handling airline administrative data, the Passenger Information and Entertainment Services Domain (PIESD), and Passenger Owned Devices (POD). He explains the physical, logical, and cryptographic isolation mechanisms separating passenger Wi-Fi and in-flight entertainment from core flight systems.

[13:29] The presentation analyzes standard avionics data buses and protocols, including unidirectional ARINC 429 buses, ARINC 664 (Avionics Full-Duplex Switched Ethernet / AFDX), and CAN bus integrations [16:28]. Madarassy examines data loading mechanisms such as ARINC 615A [19:51] used to install field-loadable software updates on Line Replaceable Units (LRUs). He concludes by discussing airworthiness cybersecurity certifications (such as DO-178C, DO-254, and DO-326A/ED-202A) and the strict safety and regulatory constraints [27:05] that govern security testing on operational aircraft.

In this presentation at the DEF CON 27 TransportHax Village, Exploding Lemur (Nick) provides an educational overview of aeronautical radio frequencies, avionics protocols, and how hackers can monitor aviation communications using low-cost Software-Defined Radios (SDR). He starts at 04:00 by detailing VHF AM voice communications across the 118–137 MHz band, explaining how Air Traffic Control (ATC) towers, automated terminal information services (ATIS), and pilot unicom channels operate.

Nick examines transponder surveillance systems at 08:00, breaking down secondary surveillance radar, Mode A squawk codes, Mode C pressure altitude encoding, and Mode S interrogation. At 12:00, he discusses ADS-B data streams broadcast over 1090 MHz and contrasts them with satellite-delivered weather services like SiriusXM Aviation. He details satellite navigation architecture at 16:00, explaining how GPS time beacons and WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System) differential signals ensure precise aircraft positioning.

At 20:00, Nick reviews Distance Measuring Equipment (DME), explaining its pulse ping-and-reply mechanics between airborne transceivers and ground stations. He wraps up at 24:00 by demonstrating how to build a dedicated dual-dongle SDR monitoring station to capture both 1090 MHz Extended Squitter and 978 MHz Universal Access Transceiver (UAT) broadcasts, highlighting essential bandpass filters and antenna considerations at 28:00. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

Harshad Sathaye explores the wireless attack surface of aircraft Instrument Landing Systems (ILS), demonstrating how commercial off-the-shelf Software Defined Radios (SDR) can be weaponized to spoof critical radio navigation signals during the final landing approach.

The presentation details the radio frequency characteristics of ILS localizer (runway horizontal alignment) and glideslope (vertical descent slope) beacons, which modulate 90 Hz and 150 Hz audio tones onto VHF and UHF carrier frequencies. Sathaye demonstrates how an attacker can manipulate the difference in depth of modulation (DDM) to exercise precise, real-time control over an aircraft's Course Deviation Indicator (CDI). He introduces the "single-tone attack," an optimized transmission technique that significantly reduces the RF power required to override legitimate airport navigation transmitters.

Sathaye showcases an automated, closed-loop ILS spoofer that dynamically tracks an approaching aircraft's GPS coordinates to adjust spoofed RF signals, stealthily altering the glidepath without triggering cockpit warning flags or receiver alarm flags. The attack was successfully validated against an FAA-certified flight simulator (X-Plane) utilizing AI-based autoland, producing off-runway touchdown offsets ranging from 18 to over 50 meters. The talk concludes with an analysis of potential mitigations, explaining why legacy analog RF navigation cannot easily be retrofitted with conventional cryptographic authentication and discussing the architectural challenges of securing next-generation aviation systems.

In this address at the DEF CON 27 TransportHax Village, Art Manion from the CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC) discusses the critical evolution of Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD), Software Bills of Materials (SBOM), and Software Origin Transparency and Authenticity (SOTA) across critical infrastructure sectors. Drawing on his extensive experience managing thousands of vulnerability disclosures at 05:00, he tracks the transformation of vendor attitudes from hostile denial toward collaborative remediation.

Art explains the multi-party coordination challenges handled by CERT/CC at 10:00, showing how vulnerabilities impacting shared libraries or hardware components ripple across interconnected supply chains. At 15:00, he examines pioneering regulatory guidance from the FDA for medical device manufacturers, illustrating how establishing post-market vulnerability handling policies creates a proven template for automotive, aerospace, and transportation safety.

Diving into supply chain visibility at 20:00, Art highlights the monumental challenge of uniquely identifying software packages across the internet, discussing Package URLs (purl) and Common Platform Enumerations (CPE). He examines SOTA frameworks at 25:00, emphasizing that securing transport systems requires knowing not just what code is running, but where it originated and whether its integrity was cryptographically preserved. He concludes at 29:00 with a roadmap for institutionalizing transparency across critical infrastructure. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

Dr. Will Roper, Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics, hosts an open discussion on modernizing military cybersecurity culture, accelerating defense software delivery, and expanding partnerships with the independent hacker community.

[04:35] Roper reflects on the evolution of military bug bounty initiatives, tracing the shift from initial institutional hesitation to the success of "Hack the Air Force." He explains why military leadership recognized the necessity of crowdsourcing external vulnerability discovery across defense networks, public websites, and enterprise systems.

[09:08] The presentation explores structural reforms in defense acquisition, highlighting agile software factories like Kessel Run. Roper emphasizes that modern warfare is driven by software speed, arguing that systems must deploy updates in days or weeks rather than multi-year acquisition cycles, with security integrated continuously rather than verified through lagging compliance audits [11:30]. He outlines plans to expand hacker access [18:25] to physical aircraft avionics, flight-line components, and satellite platforms, emphasizing that embracing transparent security research and collaborating with the hacker community is essential for national defense resilience.

In this talk at the DEF CON 27 Car Hacking Village (TransportHax), Ken Munro exposes severe security vulnerabilities across major aftermarket vehicle alarms, GPS tracking units, and remote immobilizers. He begins at 03:00 by detailing how security assessments into companion mobile applications and cloud management APIs uncovered broken object-level authorization (BOLA) and insecure direct object references (IDOR), allowing unauthenticated attackers to hijack user accounts.

Ken demonstrates the physical hazards of these flaws at 09:00, showing how an attacker could track real-time GPS locations for millions of equipped vehicles worldwide, remotely unlock car doors, sound alarms, and even send cut-off commands to shut down vehicle engines while in transit. At 12:00, he explains how incomplete vendor remediations left entire geographic regions exposed, noting that European cloud endpoints remained unpatched long after initial alerts.

Addressing the vulnerability disclosure lifecycle at 15:00, Ken contrasts cooperative vendors who patched bugs within hours against defensive manufacturers who issued legal threats. He concludes at 18:00 by warning consumers and fleet managers about misleading industry safety certifications, arguing that physical security accreditations frequently fail to evaluate underlying API and cloud backend security. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

Lennert Wouters presents a deep dive into the security architecture of Passive Keyless Entry and Start (PKES) systems, focusing on critical cryptographic vulnerabilities discovered in the Tesla Model S key fob. Wouters details the reverse engineering of the key fob hardware manufactured by Pektron, exposing the use of an obsolete, proprietary 40-bit cipher (DST40) for wireless vehicle authentication.

He explains the creation of an efficient proof-of-concept attack capable of cloning a Tesla Model S key fob in a matter of seconds using inexpensive, commercial off-the-shelf software-defined radio (SDR) equipment and an evaluation board. By intercepting challenge-response exchanges broadcast over low-frequency (LF) and ultra-high-frequency (UHF) channels, the attack rapidly recovers the cryptographic key and spoofed authentication tokens, allowing unauthorized entry and vehicle ignition.

Wouters expands on the broader automotive implications by examining FCC database filings, revealing that identical Pektron PKES modules were deployed by other luxury automotive and motorcycle manufacturers, including McLaren, Karma Automotive, and Triumph Motorcycles. He concludes with an account of the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process, detailing how Tesla responded by rolling out software updates, introducing PIN-to-Drive protection, and ultimately transitioning to stronger cryptographic key fobs.

In this technical deep dive at the DEF CON 27 Car Hacking Village (TransportHax), Aaron Cornelius from GRIMM provides a comprehensive guide to understanding and reverse engineering Unified Diagnostic Services (UDS / ISO 14229) across automotive CAN bus networks. He begins at 05:00 by explaining that while UDS standardizes high-level service requests, automotive manufacturers customize parameter identifiers, necessitating active bus interrogation to map functionality.

Aaron walks through ISO-TP (ISO 15765-2) network layer framing at 10:00, contrasting single-frame requests with multi-frame segmented packets used to transfer larger data buffers across eight-byte CAN payloads. At 15:00, he demonstrates techniques for scanning unknown CAN buses to enumerate active Electronic Control Units (ECUs), isolating diagnostic arbitration IDs, and querying software version identifiers.

Moving to active interaction at 20:00, Aaron explains diagnostic service handlers including RoutineControl (0x31) and DiagnosticSessionControl (0x10). He illustrates ECU fingerprinting at 25:00, showing how systematically cycling diagnostic sessions and observing physical resets (such as an infotainment display restarting) allows researchers to unambiguously correlate unseen CAN arbitration IDs with specific hardware modules inside the car. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

Victor Murray from the Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) addresses the critical vulnerabilities of Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS/GPS) used in autonomous ground vehicles, presenting a mobile testing methodology that complies with strict federal regulations. Murray notes that public GNSS signals lack cryptographic authentication and integrity protections, making them inherently susceptible to radio spoofing attacks.

[04:40] Murray explains the regulatory and legal challenges of GNSS security research in the United States, where over-the-air radio frequency (RF) spoofing or jamming of satellite navigation signals is illegal under federal law. To overcome this limitation without confining tests to indoor RF chambers, SwRI engineered a legal mobile GNSS spoofing apparatus. The system utilizes RF cabling, inline attenuators, and localized frequency translation boxes [09:07] placed between software-defined radios and the vehicle's onboard GPS receivers, enabling closed-loop, over-the-road vulnerability assessments on an operational Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV).

[13:39] The talk showcases live field demonstrations of dynamic spoofing attacks against the autonomous vehicle. Murray illustrates how manipulating satellite ephemeris data and time-of-flight signals induced severe navigation failures, including forced sudden lane departures, driving the UGV completely off the roadway, triggering emergency halts, and overriding path-planning algorithms. He concludes by emphasizing the urgent need for multi-sensor fusion—combining GNSS with LiDAR, radar, visual odometry, and inertial navigation systems (INS)—to detect and reject spoofed location telemetry in autonomous systems.

In this panel discussion from the inaugural Hack the Sea / Maritime Cyber Village at DEF CON 27, moderator Cris DeWitt and industry experts examine the rapidly evolving landscape of maritime cybersecurity policy, vessel operations, and regulatory oversight. The panel begins at 07:00 by examining international mandates, notably the International Maritime Organization (IMO) 2021 cyber risk management requirements and corresponding United States Coast Guard navigation safety circulars.

At 14:00, the panelists analyze cyber threat surfaces unique to commercial shipping vessels, offshore oil drilling rigs, and container port terminals. Coast Guard representatives detail their specialized incident response teams and port facility assessment programs at 21:00, discussing how military and civilian agencies coordinate during suspected operational disruptions.

The panel tackles the persistent myth of the "air-gapped" ship at 28:00, pointing out that modern vessels rely continuously on satellite VSAT communications, electronic chart display updates (ECDIS), and remote vendor engine diagnostics. At 35:00, they emphasize the need to move beyond compliance-driven checkbox mentalities toward practical security monitoring. They conclude at 42:00 by advocating for collaborative information sharing across commercial fleets to safeguard global marine supply chains. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

Josh Steinman, Senior Director for Cyber on the National Security Council (NSC), delivers an address at the Hack the Sea Village examining the strategic cybersecurity risks facing the global maritime sector, international shipping networks, and port infrastructure.

[04:02] Steinman explores how global supply chains depend heavily on maritime logistics, pointing out that commercial cargo shipping carries over 90% of global trade. He analyzes the systemic vulnerabilities created by the rapid digitalization of vessels and terminals, where legacy operational technology (OT), industrial control systems (ICS), and automated container cranes are increasingly interconnected with enterprise networks and satellite communication links without adequate security controls.

[08:40] The presentation addresses the cascading failure modes that can propagate between maritime choke points, regional electrical grids, and automated terminal logistics. Steinman outlines national cybersecurity policy initiatives coordinated by the White House and interagency partners [13:45], calling for stronger collaboration between the maritime industry, government regulators, and independent security researchers. He encourages the hacker community to bring hardware, radio, and protocol analysis into maritime environments to discover vulnerabilities before hostile nation-state actors exploit them.

In this presentation at the DEF CON 27 Hack the Sea Village (TransportHax), security researcher Weston Hecker offers candid career advice and technical strategies for transitioning into specialized penetration testing domains. Using gaming analogies at 04:00, he compares security career development to role-playing talent trees, encouraging practitioners to build foundational IT testing skills before specializing in esoteric niches like industrial control systems (ICS) or maritime infrastructure.

Weston reflects on his extensive vulnerability research at 08:00, explaining how identifying and responsibly disclosing more than twenty CVEs established his professional credibility. At 12:00, he describes the technical complexities of auditing offshore marine rigs, where cellular base stations, satellite backhauls, and industrial telemetry intersect in harsh physical environments.

He evaluates industry employment models at 16:00, comparing the fast-paced variety of billable consulting firms with internal enterprise security roles. At 20:00, Weston encourages aspiring testers to overcome initial programming intimidation by writing practical automation scripts. He closes at 24:00 with advice on managing burnout, maintaining curiosity, and finding renewed motivation by mentoring the next generation of researchers. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)
